title: Leaf clearance and debris removal
audience: Garden maintenance and clean-up workers who clear leaves, bark, twigs and general debris from lawns, beds, paths, driveways and gardens.
learningOutcomes: Choose a leaf-clearance method that suits the surface, the volume of debris and the site conditions.
Control the hazards of blowers, rakes and vacuums, including dust, noise, flying debris and slips.
Keep drains, gutters, paths and boundaries clear without spreading debris onto neighbouring property.
Recognise when debris is outside routine leaf clearance and must be referred, including roof and gutter work.

instruction.heading: What routine leaf clearance covers
instruction.body: Routine leaf clearance is the removal of fallen leaves, bark, small twigs and general garden debris from lawns, beds, paths, driveways and garden surfaces at ground level. It usually happens in the autumn, but many gardens need it through the year after windy weather or near deciduous trees. The job is straightforward, but the method matters. A crew that clears leaves quickly but spreads dust over the neighbour's car, blows debris into the stormwater drain or leaves a wet path slippery has not done the job well. The business's scope will say whether leaf clearance includes the gutters, the roof, the trees above the work area and the bin area. Unless the scope says so, do not clear gutters or roofs, and do not work at height. Those tasks need the access method and the training that apply to them, and are outside this lesson.

instruction.heading: Choosing the method
instruction.body: Choose the method for the surface and the volume. Rakes are best for lawns and beds where the leaves are damp and heavy, and they reduce the spread of dust and fine debris. Blowers are quicker on paved areas and driveways, but they move dust, seeds and fine particles and can damage plants and carry debris onto neighbouring property. Vacuums and collection tools suit small areas and fine debris. Use the least dusty method that will finish the job within the scope. Work with the wind, not against it, so that leaves do not blow back onto cleared areas. Do not use a blower near open windows, vehicles, pets or people. Where dust is visible, stop and change the method, or wet the surface lightly if the business's procedure allows it. Use a leaf-collection method that keeps the debris contained, such as a tarp or a covered trailer.

instruction.heading: Hazards: noise, dust, slips and debris
instruction.body: Blowers and vacuums generate high noise and can expose workers to fine dust, spores and seeds. Wear hearing protection that suits the noise level and eye protection against flying debris. A mask may be needed where dust is significant, and the mask must suit the hazard. Wet leaves and moss make surfaces slippery, especially on paths, steps, decking and the edges of ponds. Clear slip hazards first, and use boots with good grip. Keep the path clear of loose debris as you go so that people and equipment do not slip on leaves. Watch for sharp hidden items under leaves, such as broken glass, nails, wire and thorny stems, and handle them with the methods in the sharp-waste lesson. Keep drains and stormwater pits clear, and do not put leaves or debris into them. Stop work when visibility is poor, when the surface is too wet to stand on safely, or when debris contains anything you cannot identify.

instruction.heading: Debris that is not routine leaf clearance
instruction.body: Some debris is outside routine leaf clearance and must be referred. Heavy accumulations of dead wood or large branches, clearing that involves roofs and gutters, debris that has become mouldy, debris contaminated by animal waste or unknown material, and debris that has been dumped on the property may all need a different method, a different team or a licence holder. Mould-affected or contaminated material is not part of routine clearance and must not be cleared by the crew without the business's authorisation and the relevant controls. Where a large branch is hanging over the work area, stop and refer. Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Whether a tree needs a council permit depends on the council; one NSW council exempts trees under five metres, as an example only.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the method, the containment and the finish. A competent worker can explain why they chose a method, show the containment for the debris, identify the slip risks, and describe what debris they would refer. Escalate any gutter or roof request, any unknown or contaminated material, any dust problem that cannot be controlled, and any debris that will enter a drain or neighbouring property.

procedure: Confirm the scope: which surfaces are included, and whether gutters, roofs, high branches and bin areas are excluded.
Walk the area, identifying wet and slippery surfaces, drains, pets, vehicles, open windows and any unknown material.
Choose a method that suits the surface and the volume, and the least dusty option that will finish within scope.
Clear slip hazards first, then work from the far side of the area toward the collection point.
Use hearing protection, eye protection and a suitable mask where dust is significant.
Keep debris out of drains, stormwater pits and neighbouring property, and check the boundary as you finish.
Contain the debris on a tarp or in bags, and move it to the collection point using the approved route.
Record the area, the method, any referred debris and the client sign-off.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for the whole garden and the gutters to be cleared of leaves before a storm. The gutters are above the reach of the ground-level equipment.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is in scope, and what happens to the gutter request?
workedExamples.reasoning: Routine leaf clearance covers the ground-level areas in the scope. Gutter clearance above ground-level reach is work at height, which is outside this lesson and must be referred. Record the request, do not use a ladder or an unauthorised platform, and tell the client the gutter work needs a separately authorised method. Clear the ground-level areas and check the drains are clear.

workedExamples.situation: A blower is used on a driveway while a neighbour's car is parked close by and a child is playing near the fence.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the blower. Dust and debris from the blower are going onto the neighbour's car and toward the child, so the method is unsafe in that location. Move the child and the car's exposure out of the way, or change to raking and collection. Restart only when the area is clear, and record the stop.

equipmentAndPpe: Rakes, brooms and shovels suited to the surface
Hearing protection suitable for the noise level
Dust mask or respirator where dust is significant, selected for the hazard
Boots with good grip for wet surfaces
Blower or vacuum, inspected before use, where the method is appropriate

commonErrors.error: Using a blower in windy or close conditions and spreading dust onto cars, windows and people.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose a less dusty method, work with the wind, and stop when dust or people are near.

commonErrors.error: Clearing gutters or roof areas because the client asked, without the authorised method or scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the scope. Refer any work at height or on a roof, and record the referral.

commonErrors.error: Pushing leaves into the stormwater drain to clear the path.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep debris out of drains and pits, and collect it in containers for the approved route.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring wet, slippery paths while carrying bags of debris.
commonErrors.prevention: Clear slip hazards first, use grip footwear, and keep the route clear as you work.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Work at height, including gutter and roof clearing, needs an access method and training suited to that work. This lesson does not authorise it.
Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business.
Dust and noise exposure controls fall under the model WHS framework's duty to manage risk to the level that is reasonably practicable.

qualityStandard: The clearance covers the agreed areas, and no excluded area has been cleared.
No debris has entered a drain, a stormwater pit or a neighbouring property.
Slip hazards were cleared before the work moved on, and the route is clear at the end of the job.
Referred debris and excluded work are recorded and communicated to the client.
documentationEvidence: Scope record for leaf clearance, including exclusions for gutters, roofs and high branches.
Method record for the job, including any stop for dust, noise or slip risk.
Referral record for any debris outside routine clearance.
Client sign-off for the completed area.
summary: Leaf clearance is ground-level work. Gutters, roofs and high branches are excluded unless the scope and access method authorise them.
Choose the least dusty method that will finish the work, and keep debris out of drains and off neighbouring property.
Clear slip hazards first and watch for hidden sharps.
Refer mouldy, contaminated, large or unknown debris rather than clearing it routinely.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for the gutters to be cleared as part of a leaf clearance job. What is correct?
options: Check whether gutter work is within scope and an authorised method. If not, record the request and refer it.
Clear them with a ladder, since they are part of the garden and the crew is already on site today
Use the blower from the ground to blow the gutters clear, since the blower reaches the height easily

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker wants to use a blower on a driveway while a car is parked close and a child is nearby. What should happen?
options: Use the blower quickly, since the child is some distance away and the job will be done in a minute
Stop, move the child and car out of the exposure area, or change to raking and collection, and restart only when clear.
Ask the neighbour to move the car after the job, since the car is not in the way of the work for long

knowledgeChecks.question: Which debris should be referred rather than cleared as routine leaf clearance?
options: Dry leaves on a lawn that are easy to rake and collect into a bin
Small twigs on a gravel path, which are easy to sweep up into a pile
Mouldy or contaminated debris, or unknown material found in the pile.
